processing: Made as an Anxi oolong, with partial oxidation and rolling into tight pellets. Lots usually keep a light, fragrant style that shows off the cultivar's high aroma.
harvest_season: As with other Anxi oolongs, mainly spring and autumn.
appearance_dry: Tight pellets with the yellowest tone among the Anxi cultivars.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale gold to yellow, in keeping with the name.
appearance_wet: Thin leaves, noticeably yellower than those of the other Anxi cultivars.
taste_profile: A high, sweet floral scent of orchid and osmanthus is the point of this tea, with a cup close to Tie Guan Yin in strength but different in sweetness and aftertaste.

brewing.notes: A porcelain gaiwan shows off the perfume best. Keep steeps short and use a light hand.

vintage_note: Normally sold as the current year's spring or autumn tea, as with other lightly made Anxi oolongs, and best drunk within about a year. Some shops label it by year and region; the same plant is also sold as Huangjin Gui.
description:
Huang Dan is an Anxi cultivar, and the plant behind the oolong sold as Huangjin Gui, golden osmanthus. It is native to Anxi and belongs to the local sezhong group of oolongs other than Tie Guan Yin.

The method is the usual Anxi one, so the difference comes from the leaf. Dry pellets look yellower than their neighbours, and the wet leaves are thin and yellow as well.

The smell is what you remember: sweet, high and floral, close to orchid and osmanthus. Use very hot water and short steeps, which suit its fragrance.

It is sold under either name, and normally by the current year's harvest. The name Huang Dan points at the cultivar and is the one to look for in specialist shops; the name Huangjin Gui is the commercial one. If you like it, Chungui is a modern cultivar selected from its seedlings.
history:
Its origin comes down to us as two legends. In one, set around 1860, a bride named Wang Dan brought seedlings from her family home to Lin Ziqin's household, and the tea took a name that sounded like hers in the local speech. In the other, set around 1850, a farmer named Wei Zhen spotted a golden plant by a stream and cultivated it, naming it for its yellow colour.

The later account is more commercial: in the early twentieth century the merchant Lin Jintai sold the tea successfully in Southeast Asia and replaced the plain old name with Huangjin Gui. Dates differ between accounts. In the 1950s Anxi's grading system placed it in the sezhong group.
